title: The Treasure Fleets
eyes: Ming Veritable Records (Taizong, Xuanzong and Yingzong Shilu)
Zheng He (鄭和, born Ma He), in his dated stone inscriptions
The seventh voyage's dated itinerary ('Xia Xiyang', preserved by Zhu Yunming)
Anonymous chronicler of the Rasulid state of Yemen (Tarikh al-dawla al-Rasuliyya fi l-Yaman)
places: Carved at Nanjing; set up at Galle, Sri Lanka
With the fleet in Sri Lanka, Bengal, Sumatra and the Somali coast
Aboard the flagship's staff, seventh voyage
Aboard the main fleet, Nanjing to Hormuz and back
Nanjing, at court when the Bengal giraffe arrived
Aden and the inland court at al-Janad and Ta'izz
Cambay, Vijayanagara, Pedir in Sumatra, Java, Champa, Calicut, Aden
intro: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming court sent seven great fleets from the Yangtze into the Indian Ocean. Commanded by the palace eunuch Zheng He, a Muslim from Yunnan, the fleets of large wooden junks carried tens of thousands of soldiers, sailors, officials and interpreters to Champa, Java, Sumatra, Melaka, Sri Lanka, Calicut, Hormuz, Aden and the coast of Somalia and Kenya, distributing silks, demanding acknowledgement of the emperor, and returning with envoys, gems, spices and animals no one in China had seen. Almost nothing about the voyages survives as a diary. The fleets' own logs were later lost or destroyed, and Zheng He left only dated stone inscriptions. What remains is a set of very different documents, and this chapter is honest about their forms: the Ming Veritable Records, compiled court annals dated to the day; three books by men who sailed (the interpreter Ma Huan, the soldier Fei Xin and the secretary Gong Zhen), written up after their return and arranged by country, not by date; a day-dated route list of the last voyage that survives only because a scholar copied it decades later; a court eulogy for a giraffe; and the steles themselves. The hosts' voices are thinner, and we have tried neither to invent nor to dismiss them. A Yemeni chronicle records a Chinese envoy at the sultan's court in 1419 who would not kiss the ground. A Mamluk historian in Cairo heard in 1432 of junks at Aden asking to come to Jeddah. The Malay Annals, written down in 1612, remember China on Melaka's own terms. For Sri Lanka, whose king Zheng He captured in 1410–11, the Galle stele, cut in China with texts in Tamil and Persian, is the nearest thing to an encounter document; no participant's Sinhalese account of the capture survives. Two outsiders, the Venetian Niccolò de' Conti and the Timurid envoy Abd al-Razzaq, show the same ports just after the fleets had gone. Read together, these eyes disagree in instructive ways. The annals see tribute and ritual; Ma Huan sees markets and religions; the Yemeni court sees gift-bearing equals; the Mamluk sultan sees customs revenue; the Malay chroniclers see a Chinese emperor who must honour Melaka. Even the dates disagree: the Arabic report of Chinese ships at Aden in June 1432 does not fit the Chinese itinerary, which puts the main fleet in Java that month. The chapter's clusters are the departure of 1405, the Sri Lankan war and the visit of Melaka's king in 1409–11, the giraffes at court in 1414–15, and the last voyage of 1431–33 with the party sent to Mecca. It ends in 1436, when the court, with no more fleets to send, put the stranded envoys of ten kingdoms on a Javanese ship home.

title: Embassies to Samarkand and Beijing
places: Puerto de Santa María, near Cádiz
The Royal Camp (the Horde) outside Samarkand
Jiayuguan, western gate of the Great Wall
On the road from Cádiz to Samarkand and back
With Timur's court in western Asia
Shiraz, writing c. 1419–1425 from court records and Shami
A captive student in Samarkand during Timur's last years
In the Ottoman army at Ankara, then in Timur's following
On the road from Gansu through Moghulistan to Herat, 1414
With the embassy from Herat to Beijing and back, 1419–1422
intro: In the summer of 1402 Timur broke the Ottoman army at Ankara and captured its sultan. Kings in the far west took notice: Enrique III of Castile sent envoys east, and in May 1403 a second embassy under his chamberlain Ruy González de Clavijo sailed from Cádiz for Samarkand. At the other end of Asia, the usurping Yongle Emperor had just taken the Ming throne, and Timur, who had imprisoned Ming envoys for years, was preparing to invade China. This chapter follows the same two empires seen from opposite directions. Clavijo reached Samarkand in September 1404, in the last autumn of Timur's life, and watched Ming ambassadors humiliated at a reception before Timur marched east in midwinter and died at Otrar in February 1405. A decade later the direction reversed: under Timur's son Shahrukh, ambassadors went back and forth. The Ming official Chen Cheng logged his road to Herat day by day in 1414, and in 1419–22 the Herat painter Ghiyath al-Din Naqqash kept a diary of Shahrukh's embassy to Yongle's new palace in Beijing. The honest record here is mixed, and the forms say so. Clavijo, Chen Cheng and Naqqash kept true travel diaries, though Naqqash's survives only inside a court chronicle. The hosts speak through official histories (Shami, written for Timur; Yazdi, two decades later), the terse Ming Veritable Records, and chancery letters between Yongle and Shahrukh preserved only in Persian. Two captives, Ibn Arabshah from Damascus and Johann Schiltberger from Bavaria, wrote memoirs decades later; one is openly hostile and the other often repeats rumour. The encounters pair up. Clavijo describes Ming envoys at Timur's court; the Ming record is almost silent about Timur until the survivors of its detained missions come home. Naqqash describes the bowing, the prisoners, the emperor's fall from a Timurid horse and the lightning that burned the new halls; the Veritable Records log the tribute and the same fire. Read together, they show two courts each sure it stood at the centre of the world, and travellers working out how to bow, how far and to whom.

title: The Narrow Road
places: On the road, Nagasaki → Osaka → Kyoto → Tōkaidō → Edo
intro: In the spring of 1689 Matsuo Bashō, the most admired haikai master in Edo, sold his hut by the Sumida River and walked north with his disciple Kawai Sora. For about five months they followed the Pacific side up to Hiraizumi, crossed the mountains to the Sea of Japan, came back down the long coast of Echigo and the Hokuriku, and ended at Ōgaki in Mino. Out of it Bashō made Oku no Hosomichi, 'the narrow road to the interior', the most famous travel book in Japanese. This chapter is built on a rare gift: two records of the same journey by the two men who made it. Bashō's is not a diary. He rewrote it for years, had it fair-copied, and it was printed only in 1702, after his death. Sora's notebook, published only in 1943, is the opposite: dates, hours, distances, lodgings, weather, names — and a separate record of the verse sessions as they actually happened. Set side by side, they show where Bashō moved a date, turned fair weather into rain or rain into a starry sky, and, at Ichiburi, almost certainly invented a scene. The journey was also a chain of encounters. In nearly every town the travellers were received by a local circle of haikai poets — merchants, shipping agents, a sword-polisher, a temple abbot — and joined them in linked-verse sessions. These hosts left almost no diaries; their voices survive as their stanzas in dated session records, in letters they kept, and in the travellers' pages. That is said plainly for each of them below, and their side is not inflated beyond what survives. Two other kinds of eyes are added and flagged. Saigyō, the twelfth-century monk-poet, is not a witness at all: he is the past Bashō walked toward, the poet of the barriers and pines Bashō went to see, and his 1186 journey to Hiraizumi is recorded in a later shogunate chronicle. Engelbert Kaempfer, a German doctor of the Dutch East India Company, saw the same Japan only a year later, in 1690–92, travelling the great roads to Edo and performing before the shogun; his dates are a different year, but his foreign, counting, measuring gaze is the sharpest contrast to Bashō's. Quotations are limited to the short seventeenth-century verses themselves, given in romanized Japanese. Everything else is paraphrased; no modern translation is quoted.

title: The Transit and the Shore
eyes: Ngāti Oneone and Rongowhakaata of Tūranganui-a-Kiwa
Gweagal people of Kamay (Cooman, in family tradition)
Guugu Yimithirr people of Waalumbaal Birri
places: At sea, Society Islands and southward
West bank of the Tūranganui River
Tūranganui River and aboard the Endeavour
Aboard the Endeavour and ashore at every landing
Aboard and ashore, drawing and collecting words
intro: In August 1768 a converted Whitby collier, HM Bark Endeavour, left Plymouth with about ninety people aboard. Its public errand was astronomy: on 3 June 1769 Venus would cross the face of the sun, and timings from Tahiti, set against those from the far north, might fix the distance from the earth to the sun. Its sealed second order was to look for the great southern continent. Over the next three years the ship charted all of Aotearoa New Zealand and the east coast of Australia, nearly sank on the Great Barrier Reef, and lost a third of its people to disease at Batavia. This chapter puts the travellers' records beside those of the people they met. The British record is rich: Cook's own journal, Banks's lively and troubled one, Parkinson's posthumously published account, the surgeon Monkhouse's surviving fragment, Green's observations, Spöring's drawings. Much of it is ship's journal and log rather than private diary, and it is tagged as such. Tupaia, the Ra'iatean navigator who sailed with them, left no words, only a chart and a handful of watercolours, so he is mostly seen through others' pages. The hosts' voices survive differently, and the chapter says so plainly. Te Horeta Te Taniwha's memory of the ship at Whitianga was told when he was an old man and printed in 1888. The people of Tūranganui, the Gweagal of Kamay and the Guugu Yimithirr of Waalumbaal Birri hold their accounts in oral tradition, spoken publicly in our own time; in each case the day-by-day facts come through the British journals, while the meaning given to them by the descendants of those on the shore can be very different. Those later forms are flagged, neither inflated into contemporary records nor dismissed. Four clusters carry the chapter. The transit morning at Point Venus and Moorea, 3 June 1769. The first landing in Aotearoa at Tūranganui, 8–11 October 1769, when crew members shot and killed nine Māori people in two days, including Te Maro and Te Rākau; Banks called it the most disagreeable day of his life, and Britain expressed regret 250 years later. The landing at Kamay on 29 April 1770, where two Gweagal men stood against thirty or forty armed men. And the long stay at the Endeavour River in June–August 1770, where a quarrel over turtles ended in a ritual of peace that Guugu Yimithirr people still tell, and where English gained the word kangaroo. Read together, the journals show the voyage the way the people on board saw it, a feat of seamanship and science, and the encounters the way the shore saw them: strangers who took without asking, fired too readily, and were sometimes, for a moment, received in peace.

title: Humboldt's America
eyes: Moravian missionaries at Hopedale, Labrador (and Kapik, through them)
Indigenous guides and mission communities of the Orinoco (through Humboldt)
places: A Coruña, aboard the corvette Pizarro
Aboard a vessel in the Florida Keys
Caracas, heading south into the Llanos
Missions of the upper Orinoco and Río Negro
Havana and the interior of Cuba
From Cumaná through the Orinoco, Cuba, New Granada, Quito, Lima and New Spain to Philadelphia and Washington
At Humboldt's side for the whole journey
On a vessel in the Florida Keys, then Philadelphia
Atures, Maipures, San Fernando de Atabapo, San Carlos, the Casiquiare, Esmeralda
intro: On 5 June 1799 a Spanish mail ship left A Coruña with a Prussian mining official turned naturalist, Alexander von Humboldt, and a French botanist, Aimé Bonpland, aboard. They carried an unusual royal licence from Carlos IV that let two foreigners roam Spain's American empire with barometers, chronometers and plant presses. For five years they crossed what are now Venezuela, Cuba, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Mexico, and ended with a few crowded weeks in Philadelphia and Washington as Thomas Jefferson's guests. Humboldt's books later reshaped how Europeans pictured the Americas and how scientists thought about nature as one connected system. This chapter tries to look at that journey from more than one side. Humboldt's own record is huge: the bound field diaries (the Amerikanische Reisetagebücher, bought for the Berlin State Library in 2013 and now digitised) and dozens of dated letters, above all to his brother Wilhelm. Next to them sit the voices of the people he met. Francisco José de Caldas, a self-taught creole astronomer from Popayán, wrote dated letters full of delight and then hurt. José Celestino Mutis ran the royal botanical expedition in Bogotá. Viceroy Pedro Mendinueta sent a confidential warning to Madrid, and a Spanish naval commander filled his log with suspicion. In the United States, Jefferson wrote letters, Charles Willson Peale kept a diary and Albert Gallatin wrote to his wife. The heart of the chapter is a single night. In the small hours of 12 November 1799 the Leonid meteors came down as a storm. Humboldt and Bonpland watched from Cumaná. The American surveyor Andrew Ellicott watched from a ship in the Florida Keys, and Moravian missionaries in Labrador recorded the terror of an Inuit man named Kapik. Months later, deep in the Orinoco missions, Humboldt found that Spanish friars had written the same night into their parish books. One sky, written down in Spanish, English, German and French by strangers who never met. Honesty about form matters here. Most of the hosts' voices are letters and official papers, not diaries, and they are tagged that way. The Indigenous peoples of the Orinoco and the Andes left no known written record of these meetings. That includes the paddlers, the porters who stopped at the snow line on Chimborazo, and José de la Cruz of Cumaná, who carried the instruments for five years. They appear here only through Humboldt's pages and one painting, and the entries say so. Bonpland's own botanical journal is a run of numbered plant descriptions that are mostly undated, so much of what we know of him also comes through Humboldt. Read side by side, the sources show something Humboldt's later books smooth over. He depended on creole scientists who wanted to join him, on colonial officials who were watching him, and on Indigenous guides who knew the rivers and passes far better than he did. When he reached Washington, the first thing a President on the edge of a border quarrel with Spain wanted from him was numb

title: Ocian in View: The Corps of Discovery
eyes: Nimiipuu (Nez Perce) oral tradition of Wetxuuwíis
places: Council Bluff, near present Fort Calhoun, Nebraska
Missouri River, near present Dakota City, Nebraska
Floyd's Bluff, near present Sioux City, Iowa
Mouth of the Bad River (Wakpa Sica), present Pierre, South Dakota
Road between the Hidatsa villages and Fort Mandan
Camp Fortunate, Beaverhead River (present Clark Canyon Reservoir, Montana)
Weippe Prairie and the Clearwater (present Idaho)
Columbia estuary near Pillar Rock (present Washington)
Station Camp, north shore of the Columbia estuary
Fort Assiniboine and the Mandan and Hidatsa villages on the Knife River
Chihuahua, sending orders to Santa Fe
Weippe Prairie and the Clearwater River
Fort Mandan to the Pacific and back to the Mandan villages
intro: On 14 May 1804 a keelboat and two pirogues pushed off from Camp Dubois, opposite the mouth of the Missouri, and began rowing against the current. What makes this expedition unusual for a book about many eyes is that so many of its members wrote. Jefferson had ordered the captains to keep journals and urged others to do the same, and at least seven men did: the two captains, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, and the enlisted journalists Sergeant John Ordway, Sergeant Charles Floyd, Patrick Gass (a private who became sergeant after Floyd died), Private Joseph Whitehouse and Private Robert Frazer, whose journal is lost. Gary Moulton's edition, now online from the University of Nebraska, puts every keeper's entry for a given day on one page. So when the boats left, when Floyd died, or when Clark thought he saw the ocean, we can read four or five accounts of the same afternoon side by side. Those enlisted journals are not echoes of the captains. Ordway counts the men and the guns, Whitehouse writes down what the cook and the woodcutters did, and Gass's 1807 book (the first account of the expedition in print, heavily smoothed by his Pittsburgh editor David McKeehan) keeps the rhythm of a carpenter's working day. Where the captains write as diplomats and naturalists, the sergeants record the cost in labour, sickness and weather. The heart of this chapter is the encounter, and here the record is lopsided. The nations the Corps met (the Otoe, the Teton Lakota, the Arikara, the Mandan and Hidatsa, the Lemhi Shoshone, the Nimiipuu or Nez Perce, the Clatsop and Chinook) kept their own histories, but mostly not on paper. One dated Indigenous record does survive for these years: the Dakota winter counts, in which a keeper painted one image for each year. Lone Dog's count, kept among the Yanktonai, marks 1804–05 with a calumet dance before war and 1805–06 with eight men killed by the Crow. It does not mention the strangers on the river. That silence is itself evidence of how small the expedition looked from the plains. The Nimiipuu remember the arrival at Weippe Prairie through an oral tradition about a woman called Wetxuuwíis. It was recorded from tribal elders in 2001–02 and is flagged here as oral tradition. Sacagawea and the Mandan leader Sheheke (Big White) left no writing of their own. They appear here only through other people's pages, and their entries say so. Two rival empires were also watching. At the Mandan villages that winter, François-Antoine Larocque of the British North West Company (a 20-year-old clerk who preferred to write in English) kept a journal of his visits to Fort Mandan, where the captains warned him not to hand out British flags and medals. Far to the south, Spanish officials read the expedition as an invasion. The Commandant General of the Interior Provinces, Nemesio Salcedo, ordered New Mexico to send armed parties to find and stop the Americans. They never did. Salcedo's record is administrative: dated orders rather than a diar

title: Where the Nile Begins
places: Kaole, on the Mrima coast opposite Zanzibar
Kaole and the first marches inland
Crossing from Kabogo to Kasenge island
Uvira, north end of Lake Tanganyika
Mwanza, south shore of the Nyanza
Bagamoyo and Ugeni, on the mainland
Ripon Falls, outlet of the Nyanza
With the caravan from the Mrima coast to Kazeh and Lake Tanganyika
Lake Tanganyika and the south shore of the Nyanza
intro: In June 1857 two officers of the East India Company's armies, Richard Burton and John Hanning Speke, walked inland from the coast opposite Zanzibar to test what Arab and Swahili traders already knew: that great lakes lay beyond Unyamwezi. They reached Lake Tanganyika in February 1858, both sick, and on the way back Speke went north alone and stood on 3 August 1858 above the lake its shore-dwellers called Nyanza. He named it Victoria and declared it the source of the Nile. Burton disagreed, and the quarrel outlived one of them. Speke returned in 1860 with James Augustus Grant. They spent months at the courts of Rumanika of Karagwe, Muteesa I of Buganda and Kamurasi of Bunyoro, and on 28 July 1862 Speke watched the lake pour out over the rocks he named Ripon Falls. In February 1863 they met Samuel and Florence Baker coming upriver at Gondokoro. A public debate with Burton was arranged for the British Association at Bath on 16 September 1864. On the afternoon of the 15th Speke died by his own gun. This chapter sets the explorers' dated journals beside one another and beside the people who hosted, guided and judged them. Here the record is uneven, and the book says so. Burton's and Speke's books are edited narratives built from field journals; Speke's journal gives only day numbers, so months come from his running heads and the DNB itinerary. Grant's journals and dated watercolours survive in Edinburgh. The consul Rigby's journal survives only in a 1935 edition, and his entries are given here by month. The hosts' voices are the hardest to hear. Sidi Mubarak Bombay, the freed caravan leader who walked further than any of them, left no writing; Snay bin Amir, the Kazeh merchant who first pointed to the northern lake, survives only in Burton; Rumanika, Mutesa and Kamurasi are seen through interpreters and the travellers' prejudices. Each of these eyes is flagged. Ganda historians later wrote their own histories (Apolo Kaggwa's Basekabaka be Buganda, 1901; Ham Mukasa), and those writings remember the explorers with far less awe. They are later sources and are not used for dated entries here. Read across, the clusters show what the source of the Nile looked like on the ground: two half-blind, lame officers on a hill above Tanganyika with Bombay telling them what they were looking at; Speke at Mwanza while Burton wrote ethnography at Kazeh; a young Kabaka testing a stranger's guns; men at the falls whose thoughts no one wrote down; and in 1864 a closed debate and a short paragraph in the week's news.

title: Ujiji, 1871: Two Diaries, One Voice
eyes: David Livingstone (Unyanyembe Journal and Last Journals)
Dugumbe (Hassani) and the traders at Nyangwe
James Gordon Bennett Jr and the New York Herald
places: Zanzibar, after a visit to Bagamoyo
His camp beside the Nyangwe market, right bank of the Lualaba
Zanzibar and the mainland coast at Bagamoyo
Inside Livingstone's hut near Chitambo's village, Ilala
intro: In 1866 David Livingstone went back to Africa to answer one question: where does the Nile begin? By mid-1871 he was 58 and ill, short of men and goods, and living beside a Zanzibari slaving caravan at Nyangwe, on a great river he hoped was the Nile and which was in fact the Congo. There he saw the traders' men fire into a crowded market on a July morning and kill hundreds of people, mostly women. He turned back to Ujiji, robbed and exhausted. There a New York Herald reporter who had been looking for him for most of a year walked into the town. This chapter is built around one discovery about the record itself. Livingstone kept a raw field diary at Nyangwe, written in fading dye over a London newspaper. Later he rewrote it into a bound journal, and after his death his friend Horace Waller edited that journal into the Last Journals (1874). Between 2010 and 2012 the Livingstone Spectral Imaging Project and Livingstone Online (Adrian S. Wisnicki and colleagues) recovered the field diary. It differs from the published book: dates move, raids by his own men are toned down, his anger at the people he relied on is cut, and questions about his own followers at the massacre are dropped. Livingstone therefore appears here twice, as two eyes, so readers can set the first draft beside the public version. The second puzzle is the meeting. Both men had lost count of days through fever. Livingstone's margin says 28 October 1871, Stanley's despatch says 3 November, his book says 10 November, and historians have argued for 27 and 29 October. Livingstone's field diary stops just before the meeting, and Stanley later tore the meeting pages out of his own diary. The greeting everyone knows appears only in Stanley's printed versions, and his biographer Tim Jeal thinks it was never spoken. Most of the African voices come through European pages, and this chapter says so plainly. Dugumbe and Tagamoio, whose men fired at Nyangwe, are known only through Livingstone's accounts. Tippu Tip, who travelled with Livingstone in 1867, wrote a memoir decades later. Chuma and Susi, who decided to carry their master's body to the coast, left no writing of their own; their story reached print through Waller. Majwara, the boy alone with Livingstone when he died, was recorded by a consul. The exception is Jacob Wainwright, a freed Yao man from the Nasik mission school. He kept a diary of the death and the carrying, and its English pages were found and published only in 2019. The record here is mixed. It includes diaries, a revised journal, a posthumous edition, consular letters, newspaper reports and a late memoir, and each eye's form says which is which. The last cluster is a second dating dispute: 1 May 1873, as Waller printed it, or the night of 4 May, as Wainwright and Majwara recorded. That matches the first: the people who were present and the people who edited the record often give different answers.

title: Fram: The Ship That Drifted and the Men Who Walked
places: North of Kotelny, New Siberian Islands, c. 78°43′N
First camp, about 7–8 miles from Fram, and back
Pack ice north of Franz Josef Land
Edge of the pack, Franz Josef Land
Cape Norvegia, Jackson Island, Franz Josef Land
Fram, north of Franz Josef Land
On the ice near Cape Flora
In the ice north of Spitsbergen
intro: In June 1893 Fridtjof Nansen sailed from Christiania in a ship built to be trapped. Fram's rounded hull was designed so that the pack ice, instead of crushing her, would squeeze her upwards; Nansen's theory was that a current carried the ice from Siberia across the polar basin, and a ship frozen in north of the New Siberian Islands would drift with it towards the Pole. In late September 1893 she was frozen in. For almost three years she drifted, slowly and often backwards, with thirteen men aboard. When it became clear the drift would pass too far south of the Pole, Nansen left the ship on 14 March 1895 with one companion, the stoker Hjalmar Johansen, three sledges, 28 dogs and two kayaks. On 8 April they turned back at 86°14′, the farthest north anyone had reached. They then spent a winter in a stone hut on Franz Josef Land, living on bear and walrus, before a chance meeting in June 1896 with the English explorer Frederick Jackson at Cape Flora. Meanwhile Fram, under Otto Sverdrup, drifted on, reached her own farthest north at about 85°57′, and broke free north of Spitsbergen on 13 August 1896, the very day Nansen landed at Vardø. This chapter splits the story into two places that knew nothing of each other: the ship and the hut. Nansen's Farthest North (1897) and Johansen's With Nansen in the North (1899) give the two sides of the sledge journey, the leader's and the subordinate's; their relationship can be measured by one detail, the New Year's Eve 1895 when Nansen at last offered the familiar 'du'. Sverdrup's report, printed in Farthest North, and Bernhard Nordahl's Framgutterne (1898) follow the ship. The navigator Scott Hansen and the doctor Henrik Blessing kept diaries that stayed unpublished for over a century; the Fram Museum's 2020 edition of the crew diaries shows conflict, drinking, homesickness and sharp criticism of Nansen that his book leaves out. The encounter at the heart of this chapter is not between peoples but between two expeditions that had no idea they shared the same islands: Jackson's hut at Elmwood and Nansen's hut about a hundred miles north. Jackson's A Thousand Days in the Arctic (1899) gives the host's view of the meeting. The only Indigenous people the expedition met, the Nenets at Khabarova where the dogs came aboard, survive only through Nansen's pages; that is flagged plainly below. At the end, the London press shows how the story reached the world: by telegraph and through a newspaper's paid scoop. A note on sources: much of the record here is narrative books built from diaries rather than raw diaries, plus a ship's report, dated photographs and press reports, and the forms are tagged accordingly. A few days rest on secondary summaries and are marked 'approx'. Eva Nansen, who waited at Lysaker with their daughter Liv and came north to Hammerfest in August 1896, appears in other people's records; her own letters remain in family papers not used here, so she is not given entries of her own.

title: Two Telegrams from the Top of the World
places: Sea ice NW of Axel Heiberg Island
With Cook, on the sea ice
Sea ice, about 45 miles N of Cape Columbia
Sea ice, south toward Cape Columbia
Off Northumberland Island, aboard the Roosevelt
Lerwick, Shetland, aboard the Hans Egede
Labrador coast, on his way home
Release in New York and London (testimony taken at Etah)
Report from Greenland via Copenhagen and New York
intro: In the first week of September 1909 the world was told twice that the North Pole had been reached. On 1 September Frederick Cook cabled from Lerwick in Shetland that he had stood there on 21 April 1908. On 6 September Robert Peary wired from a Labrador fishing station that he had reached it on 6 April 1909. Each man had a small party of Inughuit, the Polar Inuit of north-west Greenland, and Peary also had Matthew Henson. Neither had any witness who could check his navigation. Within days each was calling the other a fraud. This chapter does not decide the question; the evidence it lays out has not decided it either. Peary's field diary, now in the US National Archives, has blank bound pages for 6–8 April and a loose sheet bearing the famous entry. His fast final marches and his navigation have been criticised (Dennis Rawlins, from 1973; Wally Herbert in National Geographic, 1988) and defended (Gunnar Isachsen, 1929; the Navigation Foundation's 1989 report to the National Geographic Society, which concluded he reached the vicinity of the Pole). Cook's case depends on records he said were left in Greenland, and on two companions whose testimony survives in opposite versions. The University of Copenhagen found 'no proof' in what he submitted in December 1909, and a recovered notebook copy has since been read as undermining his dates. Those are positions, reported here as positions. The heart of this volume is the encounter, and here it has an unusual shape. The hosts were the Inughuit of Avanersuaq, whose hunting, sledges, clothing and dogs made both journeys possible. Uutaaq, Siglu, Iggiánguaq and Ukujaaq stood with Peary and Henson at Camp Jesup; Aapilaq and Ittukusuk spent fourteen months with Cook. None of them left a written record. Their words reach us through Peary's and Henson's English, through a Peary Club statement taken by Cook's rivals, and through Knud Rasmussen, who questioned them in their own language and reported the reverse. We give each version and flag who recorded it. Not all the eyes here are diarists. Peary kept a field diary; Henson wrote a 1912 book built on dated diary entries; Cook's field notebooks survive only in part, and his book is a later defence; Bartlett, MacMillan and Borup are known through signed field records, manuscripts and later memoirs; Whitney through a 1910 book and telegrams; Gibbs through press dispatches; the Copenhagen committee through a dated finding. The form tags say which is which. The clusters are four: Cook's claimed day, 21 April 1908; the last week of Peary's march, 1–7 April 1909, as seen by Peary, Henson, Bartlett and Uutaaq; the five days in September 1909 when the two telegrams landed; and the autumn of testimony that ended with the Copenhagen verdict on 21 December. A quieter thread runs through them all: Ross Marvin, who never came back from the ice, and whose death was explained twice by the men who were with him.

title: Five Flags on the Ice: The Race to the South Pole

intro: In the southern summer of 1911–12 five national expeditions were at work on one continent that had no human inhabitants at all. The Norwegians under Roald Amundsen were camped at the Bay of Whales on the Ross Ice Shelf; Robert Falcon Scott's British expedition was 400 miles west at Cape Evans on Ross Island; Shirase Nobu's Japanese ship was coming south from Sydney; Wilhelm Filchner's Germans were pushing into the Weddell Sea on the far side; and Douglas Mawson's Australasians were landing on the coast south of Australia. This chapter sets their records side by side. Antarctica has no Indigenous people, so the encounters here are between the expeditions themselves and with the port towns that fed and reported them: Hobart, Sydney, Wellington, Lyttelton, Buenos Aires and Grytviken. The heart of the chapter is two meetings. On 17 January 1912, the day Scott's party reached the Pole, a day after finding Amundsen's tracks, two Norwegian officers were drinking wine aboard the Japanese ship at the Bay of Whales, talking mostly by gesture. The next day the British reached the Norwegian tent and read Amundsen's note. Both meetings are told from both sides where the record allows: the Japanese account survives as a compiled expedition record, the Norwegian one mostly as a sentence in Amundsen's book. The forms are mixed and are labelled. Scott, Wilson, Bowers, Amundsen, Bjaaland, Gran, Cherry-Garrard, Mawson and Kathleen Scott kept diaries; Prestrud's report and Filchner's narrative are dated accounts written up from journals; Shirase's 'Nankyoku-ki' (1913) is an official record compiled from members' journals; Cherry-Garrard's 'The Worst Journey in the World' (1922) is a later memoir. Scott's published journal (1913) was lightly edited, and Gran revised his diaries for publication decades later. Amundsen's book reached English readers in a 1912 translation and is paraphrased here, not quoted. The deaths are told as the diarists recorded them, without embellishment: Edgar Evans on 17 February 1912, Lawrence Oates about 16–17 March, and Scott, Wilson and Bowers in their tent at the end of March, eleven miles from a depot; then, on Mawson's journey that December and January, Belgrave Ninnis and Xavier Mertz. The tent was found on 12 November 1912, and the world learned the news on 10–11 February 1913, almost a year after the deaths and eleven months after the cable from Hobart that announced Amundsen's success. Read together, the pages show how differently the same weeks felt. On 14 December 1911 Bjaaland is eating seal steak at the Pole while Bowers needs fifteen jerks to start his sledge on the Beardmore. On 17 January Amundsen is skiing thirty miles a day homeward on a perfect crust while Scott writes the most famous sentence of the race. In March, Cherry-Garrard waits at One Ton with the dogs and the polar party struggles towards a depot it never reaches.

intro: In spring 1953 a British expedition led by John Hunt set out to put two men on the top of Everest (Chomolungma to Tibetans, Sagarmatha in Nepal) by the south route, which had only opened to outsiders when Nepal let in foreign climbers after 1949. The year before, a Swiss team had shown the way: on 28 May 1952 Raymond Lambert and Tenzing Norgay had climbed to about 8,595 m on the south-east ridge before failing oxygen and exhaustion stopped them. Behind both lay an older, separate story, told here only as a prologue: George Mallory and Andrew Irvine, last seen by Noel Odell on the north-east ridge on 8 June 1924, and never seen alive again. This chapter follows the climb through the people who wrote it down. Hillary kept a small notebook diary; Lowe wrote letters home; Evans kept a diary still unpublished, known through Harriet Tuckey's work. Much of the rest is later narrative: Hunt's official book (1953), Noyce's South Col (1954), Tenzing's Tiger of the Snows (1955, co-written with James Ramsey Ullman), and the memoirs of James Morris, the Times correspondent who later wrote as Jan Morris. Each form tag says what kind of record it is. Because these are modern copyrighted texts, every entry is a paraphrase; there are no quotations. The heart of the story is a week at the end of May. On 26 May Charles Evans and Tom Bourdillon reached the South Summit with experimental closed-circuit oxygen and turned back about 100 m short, while Hunt and the Sherpa Da Namgyal carried loads for the top camp. On 28 May George Lowe, Alfred Gregory and Ang Nyima carried to Camp IX at about 27,900 ft. At about 11.30 on 29 May Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay stood on the summit for about fifteen minutes. Then came a race of a different kind. Morris raced down the Icefall with Michael Westmacott and sent a coded message, written to read like news of failure, by runner to Namche Bazar. From there an Indian police radio sent it on to Kathmandu and London. The Times printed it on the morning of 2 June 1953, Coronation Day. The encounter at the centre of this chapter is not between explorers and strangers but between the expedition and the countries it passed through. The Sherpas who carried the loads left almost no written record of their own, and their part survives through others; this is said plainly at each point. In June 1953 the Nepali and Indian press, and crowds in the Kathmandu valley, made Tenzing a national hero and argued over whether he was Nepali or Indian and whether he had reached the top first. The entries record what each side said, without a verdict. In Kathmandu Hillary and Tenzing signed a statement that they had arrived almost together; only in 1955 did Tenzing say Hillary had stepped up first.
